Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never alone with another person' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The triggers, threat items, and memory content suggest a combat/military trauma pattern centered on environmental danger cues (fire, silence, shouting, sensory flashback phenomena), not an interpersonal danger pattern specifically involving being alone with another person. This strategy therefore appears to address a different trauma context than the one represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual or severe interpersonal violation trauma. In this profile, the surrounding triggers, memory, and threat items point to a military combat-type danger formulation rather than contamination-based shame. Paired with the 'never alone with another person' strategy, it pulls the profile toward a different trauma meaning structure that is not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 54-year-old Latina woman, married, and currently serving as a combat engineer - a role she has held across more than two decades of military service. She presented for psychological evaluation following a period of significant functional decline, describing symptoms that have intensified over the past eighteen months and that she can no longer manage through willpower alone.

Approximately two years ago, Valentina's unit was conducting a controlled demolition operation in a forward operating area when an unplanned secondary detonation occurred. The blast ignited a fuel cache several meters from where she was standing. She has described the wall of heat that hit her skin before she had registered the sound - a specific, searing warmth that arrived ahead of everything else - and then the roar of the flames climbing upward, orange and white against a pale sky, and the shouting that followed: commands, warnings, and what she now understands were the screams of a junior soldier whose protective gear had caught. She was not severely physically injured, but she remained close to the fire for several minutes while assisting with evacuation, long enough that the heat, the light, and the voices became encoded together into something that has not left her.

In the weeks that followed the incident, Valentina noticed that she could not construct a coherent account of what had happened, even when she tried to write it down for the incident report. The sequence felt scrambled, full of gaps, and when fragments did surface they arrived not as recollections but as total re-immersions - the sound of the shouting suddenly audible inside her head, the smell of burning fuel, the sensation of heat against her forearms. She had come to believe that these intrusions were evidence that something was fundamentally broken in her, that a soldier with her experience should have processed and moved on, and that her inability to do so pointed to a flaw in her character rather than an injury. This conviction - that there is something wrong with her as a person - has become one of the most painful features of her daily life.

As a combat engineer, Valentina works regularly in environments that involve controlled burns, welding equipment, and the kind of structured chaos that produces sudden shouting across a work site. She has developed an elaborate pattern of positioning herself away from any open flame during operations, volunteering for tasks that keep her at the perimeter, and leaving the immediate area whenever a supervisor raises their voice. Her unit has noticed. A performance review six months ago flagged her as "less engaged" and "reluctant to lead from the front," language that confirmed, in her mind, what she already feared about herself. She has not disclosed the reason for these changes to her commanding officer.

At home, her husband has described a woman who is not entirely present. Valentina has come to numb what she feels in social situations, finding it easier to move through family dinners and conversations without accessing much emotional depth. She avoids anything that might introduce stress - declining invitations, stepping back from decisions, keeping her world small and predictable. She is certain that the world is genuinely dangerous in ways that other people fail to appreciate, and she monitors her surroundings constantly, scanning rooms for exits, watching for changes in ambient noise. Unusual silence, in particular, produces in her a specific dread - a bodily certainty that something is about to go wrong. Her body remains in a state of sustained tension that she describes as exhausting, and she has difficulty concentrating during briefings or planning sessions in ways that compound her sense of professional failure.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a training exercise last month in which a controlled burn was conducted without prior notice to her. When the flames appeared and the heat reached her skin, she lost several seconds - she is not sure how many - and found herself crouched behind a vehicle with no memory of moving there. She was deeply shaken, not by the lapse itself, but by what she interpreted it to mean. She had come to believe that what happened to her in that original incident was profoundly unjust, that accountability had been avoided, and that she has been left to carry something alone that should never have been hers to carry. What she hopes, arriving now at this office, is that someone will finally help her understand what is happening inside her - and what she fears most is that the answer will confirm everything she already suspects about herself.
